prompt: Why does this lesson show no captured output, when lessons 9 to 12 all did?
hint: Compare what could be installed beside the other four engines.

choices.text: There is no free Oracle to run here, so it describes instead
choices.why: Inventing a session would look exactly like the real ones in the other lessons, which is what makes it worse than describing.

choices.text: Oracle's output is far too long to quote inside a lesson
choices.why: Length was never the obstacle; lesson 10 quotes plans of eleven lines and more.

choices.text: Oracle's licence forbids quoting its output
choices.why: The reason given is that there is nothing here to run, not that quoting is forbidden.

choices.text: The behaviour is identical to PostgreSQL, so the earlier captures serve
choices.why: It is not identical, and most of this lesson is about where it differs.

prompt: The lesson says the skill it teaches is not how to run Oracle. What is it instead?
hint: Think about who holds the credentials in the organisations where Oracle lives.

choices.text: Administering it well enough to cover for the DBA when needed
choices.why: A large organisation has administrators, and covering for them is not what a developer is there for.

choices.text: Writing correct SQL, and reading the contract under a decision
choices.why: Which is why the licence section comes before the dialect: most of what looks odd has money underneath it.

choices.text: Knowing the price list well enough to argue the contract
choices.why: The lesson explicitly says to look the numbers up, and the shape rather than the figure is what to carry.

choices.text: Migrating the system to PostgreSQL
choices.why: The last section treats that as a project with a budget, and often the wrong first move.

prompt: Where does the lesson say Oracle systems actually are?
hint: The common thread is a decision taken between fifteen and thirty years ago.

choices.text: Behind most public websites
choices.why: That is MySQL's installed base, from lesson 12.

choices.text: In banks, telecoms, governments and under corporate ERPs
choices.why: Systems with legal weight, bought or built long ago, that have been working since.

choices.text: In the new services being started at large technology companies
choices.why: New services are where the lesson says the choice is genuinely open, and rarely goes this way.

choices.text: On developer machines, for local work
choices.why: There is Express Edition for that, and it is not what an organisation runs.

prompt: This lesson ___ what Oracle prints rather than capturing it, and says so in the sentence each time.
hint: The opposite of capturing.

prompt: Why is the licence section placed second, before the SQL?
hint: The lesson calls the ordering its argument.

choices.text: Because most of what surprises people follows from the contract
choices.why: Where logic lives, how many environments exist, whether anybody may measure: contract first, engine second.

choices.text: Because the licence is harder than the SQL and should be met while fresh
choices.why: Difficulty is not the ordering; the licence is the explanation the later sections need.

choices.text: Because the SQL is nearly identical to PostgreSQL and needs little space
choices.why: The dialect section is long and has three traps that change what a query means.

choices.text: Because the reader may decide not to continue once the price is known
choices.why: The lesson is for somebody who has already joined an organisation that runs it.

prompt: In Oracle's vocabulary, what is the difference between an instance and a database?
hint: One of them holds no data at all.

choices.text: The instance is memory and processes; the database is the files
choices.why: The instance starts and stops and holds nothing. The database holds everything and runs nothing.

choices.text: The instance is the files on disk; the database is the running program
choices.why: Reversed. The word that means the files is database.

choices.text: The instance is a schema; the database is the server
choices.why: A schema is a user in Oracle, and is a third thing again.

choices.text: They are two words for one thing, kept apart for historical reasons
choices.why: The separation is load-bearing: with Real Application Clusters several instances open one database.

prompt: What is a schema in Oracle?
hint: It is not a namespace you create separately.

choices.text: A user
choices.why: Creating the user PAYROLL creates the schema PAYROLL, and its tables are PAYROLL.EMPLOYEES.

choices.text: A namespace inside a database, as in PostgreSQL
choices.why: That is the PostgreSQL model, where one database holds many schemas and a schema is not a login.

choices.text: A pluggable database
choices.why: A pluggable database is a level above, and holds schemas.

choices.text: A tablespace
choices.why: A tablespace is where data is stored physically, which is a different question.

prompt: An architect proposes putting three applications into three pluggable databases in one container rather than on three servers. What is the argument most likely to be about?
hint: The lesson calls it a decision wearing an architecture diagram.

choices.text: The licence, which is bought for the machine underneath
choices.why: Three servers is three sets of processor licences; one container on one machine is one.

choices.text: Isolation, since a pluggable database is weaker than a separate server
choices.why: A real consideration, and not the one the lesson names as driving this shape.

choices.text: Upgrades, since pluggable databases upgrade together
choices.why: True and secondary; the container does share an instance.

choices.text: Backup, since one container is one backup
choices.why: Convenient and not the reason the lesson gives for this shape being common.

prompt: Match each Oracle edition to what it is.
hint: One is free and capped, one is limited by server size, one is what a corporation runs.

pairs.right: free, with published caps on data, memory and CPU
a hard limit on server size, and few of the priced options
licensed per processor, with the options priced on top

prompt: Which Oracle release does the lesson say to expect in the field, and why?
hint: The release naming went from i to g to c to ai, and one release in that sequence is where systems stopped.

choices.text: 11g, because it is what most systems were built on
choices.why: Many were, and the lesson names a later one as where systems standardised.

choices.text: 23ai, because it is the current line
choices.why: It is the current line, which is not the same as the one in production in most organisations.

choices.text: 12c, the release that introduced the pluggable databases
choices.why: It did, and it is not the release the lesson says to expect.

choices.text: 19c, the long-term support release of the 12c line
choices.why: An enormous number of systems standardised on it, which is why it is what to expect.

prompt: A server has two sockets of sixteen physical cores each, with an x86 core factor of 0.5. How many processor licences does that need?
hint: Cores, times the factor, rounded up.

prompt: Why does a corporate Oracle system often have no reporting replica, with reports running at night against production?
hint: A second machine is not free here in a way it is elsewhere.

choices.text: Oracle has no replication technology you could build one with
choices.why: Data Guard exists, and reading from it while it applies is Active Data Guard, an option.

choices.text: A second server is a second set of licences
choices.why: Which makes a replica a line in a budget rather than a configuration change.

choices.text: Reports are faster on the primary because the data is warm
choices.why: A cache argument that does not survive the contention a report puts on production.

choices.text: Replicas lag too far behind to be useful for reporting
choices.why: They keep up well enough for that; the obstacle in the lesson is the bill rather than the lag.

prompt: You want to know which query is slow, and somebody says to look at the AWR report. What is the question to ask first?
hint: The views will answer whether or not you are entitled to ask them.

choices.text: Whether the report covers the window when it was slow
choices.why: Worth asking second. The first question is whether you may run it.

choices.text: Whether you have the privilege to query those views
choices.why: Close, and a grant is not the obstacle that makes this a compliance question rather than a technical one.

choices.text: Whether the statistics have been gathered recently
choices.why: A real question about plans, and a different one from whether you may read the performance history.

choices.text: Whether the Diagnostics Pack is licensed here
choices.why: AWR is that pack. On a system without it, querying the views is a licence violation rather than an error.

prompt: Which of these are separately priced options on Oracle Enterprise Edition that come built in on PostgreSQL? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four of the five are things a PostgreSQL user never thinks about buying.

choices.text: Partitioning
choices.why: Built into PostgreSQL, priced here.

choices.text: The performance history that tells you which query is slow
choices.why: The Diagnostics Pack. PostgreSQL's pg_stat_statements is free and installed.

choices.text: Reading from a standby
choices.why: Active Data Guard. A PostgreSQL streaming replica serves reads without anybody buying anything.

choices.text: Table compression
choices.why: Advanced Compression. PostgreSQL compresses large values without an option.

choices.text: Foreign key constraints
choices.why: Part of the engine on every database in this course, including Oracle.

prompt: What does the lesson say to do about the actual prices?
hint: It gives a magnitude and then a warning about it.

choices.text: Memorise the per-processor figure, which has been stable for years
choices.why: The structure is stable and the numbers move, which is why the lesson says not to trust its own.

choices.text: Look them up, and carry the shape rather than the figure
choices.why: Per core, support annual and recurring, options extra, and a second environment a second bill.

choices.text: Ask Oracle, since the price list is not published
choices.why: It is published; the lesson says to consult it.

choices.text: Ignore them: a developer does not see the contract anyway
choices.why: The whole section is about how the contract reaches decisions a developer does see.

prompt: A team's report takes ninety seconds and somebody proposes doubling the server's cores. On Oracle, what is different about that proposal compared with the same one on PostgreSQL?
hint: Count what doubling the cores doubles.

choices.text: No difference; the hardware costs the same either way
choices.why: The hardware does. The licence attached to it does not.

choices.text: Oracle does not benefit from more cores, so the report stays at ninety seconds
choices.why: It parallelises perfectly well; the objection is the bill rather than the benefit.

choices.text: It doubles the licence, so the answer is to tune the query
choices.why: A good engineering answer being reached for a reason that is not engineering, which is the section's point.

choices.text: The core factor makes extra cores free above a threshold
choices.why: The factor scales the count rather than capping it; more cores is more licences.

prompt: What happens on Oracle when you insert an empty string into a nullable text column?
hint: It is the biggest difference in the language and has no equivalent elsewhere in this course.

choices.text: The column holds an empty string, as on the other engines
choices.why: That is the other three. Oracle does not have an empty string distinct from null.

choices.text: The insert is refused, because an empty string is not a valid value
choices.why: It is accepted. What it stores is null.

choices.text: The column is null, because the empty string is null
choices.why: So `city IS NULL` is true for that row, and a NOT NULL constraint would have refused the insert.

choices.text: The column holds a single space, by the old fixed-width rule
choices.why: That is CHAR padding, which is a different behaviour and not this one.

prompt: An application ported to Oracle stops being able to tell a blank city from a city nobody gave. What has happened, and what is the fix?
hint: Two states became one, and no amount of application code can separate them again.

choices.text: A CHECK constraint on the column is rejecting the blank; drop it
choices.why: No constraint is involved; the empty string became null on the way in.

choices.text: The column type is wrong; VARCHAR2 should be CHAR
choices.why: CHAR pads to a fixed width, which changes comparisons and does not restore the distinction.

choices.text: The empty string became null, so a sentinel value is needed
choices.why: Something like a single space or an explicit marker, decided deliberately, because the engine will not keep the distinction.

choices.text: The driver is trimming the value; configure it not to
choices.why: The behaviour is the engine's and documented, not a driver setting.

prompt: `WHERE ordered_on = DATE '2026-03-19'` is a bug on Oracle and not on the other three. Why?
hint: Compare what Oracle's DATE holds with what the others' holds.

choices.text: Oracle compares dates as text, so the format has to match
choices.why: A DATE literal is a date, not a string, and the comparison is not textual.

choices.text: Oracle's DATE carries a time, so midnight rows match
choices.why: It is closer to the others' timestamp. A half-open range over the day is the fix, and it keeps the index.

choices.text: Oracle requires TO_DATE around a date literal
choices.why: The DATE literal is valid; the problem is what the column holds.

choices.text: Oracle stores dates in the session's time zone, so the value shifts
choices.why: Time zones are a real subject and a DATE has none; the time component is the issue here.

prompt: `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ROWNUM <= 3 ORDER BY ordered_on DESC` does not return the three most recent orders. What does it return?
hint: Ask when ROWNUM is assigned relative to the sort.

choices.text: The three oldest orders, since ROWNUM counts up from the other end
choices.why: It does not count from either end of the sort; it is assigned before the sort happens.

choices.text: An error, because ROWNUM does not combine with ORDER BY
choices.why: It runs and returns rows, which is what makes it a bug rather than an error.

choices.text: Whatever three rows came out first, sorted among themselves
choices.why: ROWNUM is assigned before the sort. FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY does the intended thing on 12c and later.

choices.text: A random three of the most recent ten
choices.why: There is no sampling; it is the first three the query happened to produce.

prompt: Oracle's SELECT has always required a FROM, so there is a one-row table in every database called ___ to select from when you have nothing to select from.
hint: Four letters, and it looks like a joke until you need it.

prompt: Match each Oracle plan operation to what lesson 10 called it on PostgreSQL.
hint: The names moved and the operations did not.

prompt: Which of these is a pleasant surprise rather than a trap, according to the lesson?
hint: Compare it with what SQLite did to the same column in lesson 12.

choices.text: DUAL means a FROM clause is optional
choices.why: The opposite: DUAL exists because a FROM is required.

choices.text: The empty string is null, which keeps blank data out by accident
choices.why: It is the largest trap in the language, and it removes a distinction rather than protecting one.

choices.text: ROWNUM makes pagination simple
choices.why: It is the section's bug, assigned before the sort.

choices.text: NUMBER is an exact decimal, so a money column is exact by default
choices.why: NUMBER(10,2) is what lesson 3 asked for, and floating point has to be asked for by name.

prompt: What is PL/SQL?
hint: It is not a dialect of SQL.

choices.text: A procedural language inside the database, with SQL in it
choices.why: Variables, loops, exceptions and procedures, with SELECT and UPDATE as statements rather than strings.

choices.text: Oracle's name for its SQL dialect
choices.why: The dialect is SQL. PL/SQL is a separate procedural language that contains SQL.

choices.text: A client library for calling Oracle from an application
choices.why: That is a driver, and it lives on the application's side.

choices.text: A query builder that generates the SQL from chained method calls
choices.why: That is lesson 11's layer, and it runs in the application.

prompt: What does declaring a variable as `orders.status%TYPE` buy you?
hint: Compare it with the drift lesson 11 described between a class and a table.

choices.text: It ties the variable to the column's value, and refuses assignment
choices.why: It ties the type, not the value; the variable is ordinary otherwise.

choices.text: It validates the value against the column's CHECK constraint
choices.why: The constraint applies when a row is written, not when a variable is assigned.

choices.text: It locks the column's definition while the procedure runs
choices.why: Nothing is locked; it is a compile-time reference to the type.

choices.text: It takes the column's type, so a change to it follows through
choices.why: The opposite of a class that names a type and silently disagrees with the table after a migration.

prompt: `SELECT status INTO v_status FROM orders WHERE id = p_order_id` finds no row. What happens?
hint: A whole class of silent wrongness is an exception here.

choices.text: The variable is left null and the procedure carries on
choices.why: That is the silent behaviour the construct deliberately does not have.

choices.text: `NO_DATA_FOUND` is raised
choices.why: And more than one row raises TOO_MANY_ROWS, which is the other half of the same guarantee.

choices.text: The procedure returns immediately with no error
choices.why: Nothing returns quietly; an exception is raised and has to be handled or propagated.

choices.text: The variable keeps whatever it held before
choices.why: Oracle raises rather than leaving a stale value, which is the point of the INTO form.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson give as reasons the logic ended up inside the database? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three were good arguments at the time and one was the tooling.

choices.text: One place for a rule that six applications and a batch all have to obey
choices.why: The same argument lesson 11 made for a constraint over a class validation, taken further.

choices.text: A loop inside the server sends no statements across a network
choices.why: The N+1 problem solved by moving the loop, and on 1998 hardware a large win.

choices.text: The database is the machine the licence already paid for
choices.why: Work done there is work on hardware already bought, which is the licence section again.

choices.text: Oracle Forms and the tools of that era assumed logic lived there
choices.why: Named as the one reason that was not good: the path of least resistance rather than a decision.

choices.text: PL/SQL runs faster than the same logic compiled in any application language
choices.why: Not a claim the lesson makes; the network argument is about round trips rather than raw speed.

prompt: You join a team whose Oracle system has a thousand PL/SQL packages. What does the lesson advise?
hint: It is explicit about what not to start doing.

choices.text: Read them as the documentation of the business, and move little
choices.why: They are usually better documentation than anything written down, and the constraints stay in the tables either way.

choices.text: Move the logic out to the application, where it can be tested and reviewed
choices.why: Both costs are real and the lesson says not to move things because they are unfashionable.

choices.text: Leave them entirely alone, since nobody can review PL/SQL safely
choices.why: Reviewing is a discipline the lesson names, not an impossibility.

choices.text: Rewrite them in the application's language before adding anything new
choices.why: That is the migration project of the last section, proposed with no reason to migrate.

prompt: What is a package, and why does the lesson call it the unit that matters?
hint: It has two parts, and one of them is private.

choices.text: A file of procedures kept in version control and loaded at start-up time
choices.why: The deployed version lives in the database, which is exactly the review problem the lesson names.

choices.text: A transaction boundary around a set of statements
choices.why: Transactions are the procedure's; a package is a unit of code rather than of work.

choices.text: A compiled query plan Oracle keeps for reuse
choices.why: That is the shared pool, and it is the subject of the bind-variable section.

choices.text: A group of procedures with a specification and a private body
choices.why: A corporate system's API is often a set of packages, and the application calls them without writing SQL.

prompt: Oracle offers read committed and serializable. Which of lesson 8's levels is impossible on it by construction, rather than merely not offered?
hint: Ask what a reader is served from, and whether there is anything for it to expose.

choices.text: Read uncommitted
choices.why: A reader is served from undo, so there is no uncommitted version for it to see. The level has nothing to expose.

choices.text: Read committed
choices.why: It is the default, so it is offered rather than absent.

choices.text: Repeatable read
choices.why: Also not offered by name, and not impossible: serializable is stronger and gives what it would have. The question is about what cannot exist.

choices.text: Serializable
choices.why: Offered, and the stronger of the two Oracle has.

prompt: A two-hour report fails partway through with `ORA-01555`. What has happened?
hint: The query was reading as of when it started. Ask where those old versions were kept.

choices.text: The query held a lock too long and was chosen as a deadlock victim
choices.why: That is ORA-00060, and readers do not take the locks that deadlock.

choices.text: The undo it needed had been recycled, so Oracle refused
choices.why: The report was correct and the system could not keep its promise. Reporting it to the DBA with the statement and start time is the right move.

choices.text: The report exceeded a configured maximum query duration
choices.why: There is no such timeout in play; the error names a snapshot and a segment number.

choices.text: Another transaction committed a change the report had already read
choices.why: That is ordinary and read consistency handles it; the failure is that the old version was no longer reconstructible.

prompt: A migration script of six `ALTER TABLE` statements fails on the fourth, inside a transaction. What is left behind on Oracle?
hint: Lesson 12 captured the same behaviour on MySQL.

choices.text: The old schema; the transaction rolled the first three back
choices.why: DDL issues an implicit commit before and after itself, so there was nothing left to undo.

choices.text: The first three changes, committed as they ran
choices.why: Which is why an Oracle migration is one reversible step at a time, with a tool that can resume.

choices.text: The new schema, since a failed ALTER is skipped and the rest continue
choices.why: The fourth failed and the ones after it never ran.

choices.text: The schema is left locked for the session that failed
choices.why: Nothing is left locked; a half-applied schema is the damage.

prompt: An application hangs waiting on a row lock. The lock is held by a colleague's client window. What is the likely cause?
hint: Oracle's server does not commit for you.

choices.text: Their session crashed and the lock was orphaned
choices.why: A crashed session is rolled back and its locks released; a live one holding an open transaction is not.

choices.text: They ran a SELECT, which takes a shared lock on the rows read
choices.why: A plain read takes no row lock on Oracle and never blocks a writer.

choices.text: They ran an UPDATE before lunch and did not commit or roll back
choices.why: Every statement opens a transaction that stays open, and SQL*Plus does not commit by default.

choices.text: Their isolation level is serializable, which locks everything it reads
choices.why: Serializable on Oracle is implemented with read consistency rather than read locks.

prompt: Oracle serves a long query from the ___ area, which is how a reader never blocks a writer and never sees uncommitted work.
hint: Four letters, and the section's error message is about it running out.

prompt: What does `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` do, and when does the lesson say to want it?
hint: Think about what a user staring at a screen is being told.

choices.text: It takes the lock without waiting for the other session to commit
choices.why: It does not skip the other session's lock; it declines to queue behind it.

choices.text: It fails at once rather than waiting, so a screen says why
choices.why: Better served than a user watching a spinner with no idea what is happening.

choices.text: It releases the lock as soon as the statement finishes
choices.why: Row locks are held until commit or rollback, as everywhere else in this course.

choices.text: It skips locked rows and returns the rest
choices.why: That is SKIP LOCKED, which is a different clause and a different intent.

prompt: What is the productive way to bring a performance problem to a DBA?
hint: One of these is a conversation and the rest are not.

choices.text: The statement, its plan, the counts, and what should change
choices.why: A specific request with its evidence. The lesson contrasts it with "the database is slow".

choices.text: A ticket saying the database is slow, with the screen that was affected
choices.why: Named as the version that is not a conversation; the screen runs several statements.

choices.text: A request for SYSDBA so you can look yourself
choices.why: You will not have it and should not, and most of what you need is a grant.

choices.text: A benchmark comparing the system with PostgreSQL
choices.why: It answers a question nobody is asking about a system nobody is going to swap this quarter.

prompt: Match each Oracle tool to what it does.
hint: One is the client, one is the backup, one is the standby, one is the performance history.

pairs.right: a standby kept current from redo
the performance history, part of a priced pack

prompt: Which view is the Oracle counterpart of `pg_stat_statements` from lesson 10?
hint: Oracle exposes its internal state as views with a distinctive prefix.

choices.text: `V$SESSION`
choices.why: It shows who is connected and what they are waiting on, which is a different question.

choices.text: `V$LOCK`
choices.why: It shows the locks, which answers the hang from the last section rather than this one.

choices.text: `V$SQL`
choices.why: The statements in the shared pool with their execution counts and elapsed times.

choices.text: `DBA_TABLES`
choices.why: A data dictionary view about the schema rather than about statements that ran.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a major-version upgrade is a project rather than a task?
hint: Count what has to be re-certified around the database.

choices.text: Because the data has to be exported and reloaded each time
choices.why: That is not what an Oracle major upgrade requires; the work is around the database.

choices.text: Because the licence has to be renegotiated at each major version
choices.why: Not a claim the lesson makes; the licence is per processor and perpetual.

choices.text: Because every application that connects has to be certified first
choices.why: Which is part of why 19c is so widely deployed: it was a defensible place to stop.

choices.text: Because Oracle only supports upgrades performed by its own consultants
choices.why: No such requirement appears; the obstacle is certification and testing.

prompt: You find a query online that uses `FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY` and it fails on your system. What is the first thing to check?
hint: Lesson 12 made the same point about advice found online.

choices.text: Whether the table has more than ten rows
choices.why: It returns fewer rows rather than failing when there are fewer.

choices.text: Whether your user has the privilege to run it
choices.why: There is no privilege attached to a syntax clause.

choices.text: Which Oracle version you are on: that clause needs 12c
choices.why: Advice about Oracle spans twenty-five years of releases and often does not say which one.

choices.text: Whether the Diagnostics Pack is licensed
choices.why: That gates the performance history rather than the SQL you may write.

prompt: Four hundred lookups by four hundred different e-mail addresses arrive with the values glued into the statement text. What does Oracle do?
hint: Ask what makes two statements the same statement to the engine.

choices.text: It recognises the shape and reuses one plan
choices.why: Only with cursor sharing forced on, which is a workaround for this rather than the default behaviour.

choices.text: It refuses after a configured number of distinct statements
choices.why: Nothing refuses; the cost is spread across the system, which is what makes it hard to see.

choices.text: It caches the results, so the second four hundred are fast
choices.why: The result cache is a different mechanism and these are four hundred different results anyway.

choices.text: It hard-parses four hundred statements and fills the shared pool
choices.why: Parsing is expensive, it takes latches everything else wants, and the whole database slows with no single query looking slow.

prompt: A bind variable is the same practice lesson 11 taught. What did lesson 11 want it for?
hint: One practice, two payoffs.

choices.text: To let the ORM map types correctly between the language and the column
choices.why: A separate benefit of a mapper, and not what the parameter itself is for.

choices.text: To make a query's plan stable across runs
choices.why: Stability is a consequence here, and it was not lesson 11's argument.

choices.text: To allow a statement to be reused across connections
choices.why: Sharing across sessions is the shared pool's doing, not the parameter's purpose.

choices.text: To keep SQL injection impossible: statement and value apart
choices.why: On Oracle it is also the difference between a system that scales and one that does not.

prompt: The lesson names one honest exception to always using a bind variable. What is it?
hint: It is about a column whose values are wildly unequal in how many rows they match.

choices.text: A heavily skewed column, where values want different plans
choices.why: A bind hides the value at parse time. Oracle has adaptive cursor sharing and bind peeking for it, and it is not a reason to concatenate.

choices.text: A column used in an ORDER BY, where the planner needs to know the direction
choices.why: The direction is in the statement text either way; it is never a bound value.

choices.text: A very large table, where the planner needs the literal to estimate the size
choices.why: Size comes from statistics about the table rather than from the value in the predicate.

choices.text: A column with no index, where a literal lets the planner skip the index check
choices.why: The planner checks what indexes exist regardless of how the value arrived.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson say are fully yours as a developer, needing no privilege, licence or meeting? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four of the five need nobody's permission.

choices.text: The SQL you write
choices.why: Most of the performance, and entirely in your hands.

choices.text: Using bind variables
choices.why: Most of the rest of the performance, and free.

choices.text: Your transaction boundaries, including how long one stays open
choices.why: Which is the last section's support call and lesson 8's argument.

choices.text: Keeping a function off an indexed column in a WHERE
choices.why: Lesson 9, and it costs nothing.

choices.text: Running the AWR report over the slow window
choices.why: That may need the Diagnostics Pack licence, which is exactly what is not yours to decide.

prompt: A screen is slow against an Oracle you do not administer. Put the steps in the order the lesson would have you take them.
hint: Everything you can do alone comes before anything you have to ask for.
items: Find which statement the screen actually runs, and how often
Check that it is sent with bind variables rather than glued-in values
Get its plan and put estimated against actual rows on every line
Take the statement, the plan and the counts to the DBA with a proposal
trap: Asking for an index first is the common order, and it arrives without the evidence that would say whether an index is the answer.

prompt: A table is bulk-loaded overnight and a query against it plans badly in the morning. What is a specific question worth asking?
hint: Oracle's planner depends on the same thing PostgreSQL's does.

choices.text: Whether the table should be partitioned
choices.why: An option that has to be licensed, and a large change proposed before the cheap explanation was checked.

choices.text: Whether the load should run during the day instead
choices.why: It moves the problem into business hours without addressing why the plan is wrong.

choices.text: Whether the statistics were gathered since the load
choices.why: A planner on yesterday's numbers estimates today's table wrongly, and this is legitimate and specific.

choices.text: Whether the shared pool is large enough
choices.why: A real tuning subject and not the one a stale-statistics plan points at.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson name as something Oracle is genuinely good at?
hint: One of them is not a technical property at all, and the lesson says so.

choices.text: Read consistency with no process reclaiming dead row versions
choices.why: The undo design removes a class of PostgreSQL operational work, and ORA-01555 is its price.

choices.text: Being cheaper than the alternatives at scale
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson supports that; the licence section is the opposite argument.

choices.text: Being easier to operate with a small team
choices.why: It has a role dedicated to operating it, which is the shape of the opposite claim.

choices.text: Having the most portable SQL of any engine in this whole course
choices.why: Its dialect has DUAL, ROWNUM, NVL and the empty-string rule, which the migration table lists as work.

prompt: A new internal service needs a few hundred gigabytes and a few thousand transactions a minute. Somebody proposes putting it on the corporate Oracle because the licence already exists. What does the lesson call that?
hint: It has a name in this section, and it is about which direction the bill moves.

choices.text: A reasonable reuse of capacity that is already paid for
choices.why: The capacity is what is paid for; adding load to it is how the next licence gets bought.

choices.text: The correct call, since operating one engine is cheaper than two
choices.why: A real consideration, and not one that survives ordinary requirements and a per-core bill.

choices.text: Inertia: ordinary requirements, and the licence deciding again
choices.why: A new service with no exotic need is a PostgreSQL service, whatever is already running.

choices.text: A compliance risk, since a new application needs its own licence
choices.why: The licence is per machine rather than per application; the objection is cost rather than compliance.

prompt: In a migration off Oracle, which part does the lesson call the project?
hint: Two rows of its table are in bold, and one of them is code.

choices.text: Moving the schema and the data
choices.why: Tooling exists and that part is largely mechanical.

choices.text: Translating the DUAL, ROWNUM, NVL and SYSDATE in the code
choices.why: Mechanical and tedious, which is not the same as being the project.

choices.text: Replacing the backups and the monitoring
choices.why: Real work, and it is operational practice rather than the thing with no tool.

choices.text: Rewriting the PL/SQL packages, which no tool does for you
choices.why: The business logic has to be rewritten and re-tested, and that is where the budget goes.

prompt: Why is the empty string given its own row in the migration table, when the rest of the dialect is called mechanical?
hint: Ask what the application could express before the migration, and what it could express on Oracle.

choices.text: Because no target engine has an equivalent of it
choices.why: Every other engine has both an empty string and a null; that is the direction the problem comes from.

choices.text: Because the values have to be re-encoded on the way out
choices.why: The bytes move fine; it is the missing distinction that does not.

choices.text: Because CHECK constraints on those columns will not port
choices.why: Constraints port readily, and this row is about data rather than about schema.

choices.text: Because the blank-against-absent distinction was never stored
choices.why: Every place that distinction mattered has to be found and decided, and no rule recovers what was never stored.

prompt: The lesson names an intermediate move that is often the real one. What is it?
hint: It is less satisfying than a migration and is what usually happens.

choices.text: Move the reporting off first, and leave the transactional system alone
choices.why: A sensible step, and not the one the lesson names.

choices.text: Stop adding to it, and let the surface shrink over years
choices.why: Less satisfying than a migration, and what usually happens.

choices.text: Downgrade to Standard Edition 2 to cut the bill
choices.why: It changes the bill and the available features; the lesson does not propose it.

choices.text: Move to Oracle's cloud service, where the licence is included
choices.why: Not a move the lesson discusses.

prompt: What are the three things the lesson says to leave with?
hint: One is about the course, one is about money, and one is about you.

choices.text: That Oracle should be avoided, that licences are unfair, and that PostgreSQL is better
choices.why: None of those is in the section, which spends its first half on what Oracle is good at.

choices.text: That the DBA decides everything, that the licence decides the rest, and that little is in your hands
choices.why: The opposite of the third point, which lists what needs no privilege, licence or meeting.

choices.text: That PL/SQL should be learned, that the AWR should be read, and that RAC is worth having
choices.why: Three specifics from the middle of the lesson rather than what it closes on.

choices.text: That the engine is not the subject, that money is an input, and that the query is yours
choices.why: The most different engine in the list, and the difference was contract, vocabulary and operations rather than what a correct query is.

prompt: Lesson 12 said the tools change and the ___ do not, and this lesson calls itself the strongest case of that.
hint: One word, plural.

prompt: An internal system has forty known users and nothing a customer can reach. Which licence metric may fit, and what rules it out elsewhere?
hint: One metric counts machines and the other counts people.

choices.text: Named User Plus, which needs the population to be known and bounded
choices.why: It is priced per user with a published minimum per processor, and anything the public reaches has no such count.

choices.text: Processor, since forty users is a small machine
choices.why: That one ignores users entirely and prices the cores, whoever is using them.

choices.text: Express Edition, which is free for any user count
choices.why: It is free and capped on data, memory and threads, which is a different limit from the metric.

choices.text: Either; the two are priced identically at this size
choices.why: They are different metrics with different arithmetic, and which is cheaper depends on both numbers.

prompt: On Oracle a schema is a user, so the same table name means different tables to different logins. What papers over that?
hint: Something you create so one name reaches another owner's table.

choices.text: A synonym for the other owner's table
choices.why: It gives one name that resolves elsewhere, and a corporate schema usually has a great many.

choices.text: A schema search path, as in PostgreSQL
choices.why: There is no namespace below the user there for a path to search.

choices.text: A view over the other owner's table
choices.why: It would work and it is a second object to keep in step with the first.

choices.text: A grant on the table
choices.why: Necessary before either of the others, and it does not change how the name resolves.

prompt: Somebody compiled a change to a package straight into the database rather than through the repository. What is now true?
hint: Ask where the deployed version lives.

choices.text: The change will be lost at the next restart
choices.why: It is compiled and stored; a restart does not undo it.

choices.text: The repository is wrong and nothing reports it
choices.why: What runs lives in the database, so keeping the two in step is a discipline rather than a property.

choices.text: The package is now invalid until it is recompiled
choices.why: It compiled, which is what makes this silent.

choices.text: The next deploy will refuse, having found a difference
choices.why: Nothing is comparing the two, which is the whole difficulty.

prompt: On Oracle, `TRUNC(ordered_on) = DATE '2026-03-19'` finds the right rows where a bare equality does not. Why is a range still the better answer?
hint: An argument from lesson 9, unchanged by the engine.

choices.text: Because a range is easier to read
choices.why: That is arguable in both directions and is not the reason.

choices.text: Because the function around the column defeats an ordinary index on it
choices.why: The sorted copy holds the column's values and not the function's, exactly as on the engines of lesson 9.

choices.text: Because that function is not available in older releases
choices.why: It is old and present everywhere; availability is not the objection.

choices.text: Because the equality would match rows at midnight only
choices.why: True of the bare equality, and this one already fixes that.

prompt: A separately-priced option was switched on once by somebody trying it, and switched off again. What does the contract make of that?
hint: Ask what an audit measures: use, or intent.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as it is off when an audit happens
choices.why: Use is what is found, and turning it off afterwards does not unmake it.

choices.text: Nothing; trying a feature is covered by the edition
choices.why: The options are priced on top of the edition, which is why they are listed separately.

choices.text: It is use, and an audit bills for the licences and the back support
choices.why: That mechanism is why a developer asking to enable something is asked why rather than told yes.

choices.text: It is use, and the bill is capped at one year
choices.why: Back support is what makes the exposure longer than the moment.

prompt: A two-hour report fails partway through because the versions it needed had been recycled. Half the answer belongs to the person who runs the database. What is the other half, which is yours?
hint: The exposure grows with how long the reading goes on.

choices.text: Retry it until the system is quiet enough
choices.why: It may work and it leaves the report just as exposed tomorrow.

choices.text: Make it read for less time, by splitting it or making it faster
choices.why: The promise is about the moment it started, so a shorter read is less to keep.

choices.text: Move the report to a standby that nobody writes to
choices.why: Reading a standby while it applies is a priced option, and the reading is still long.

choices.text: Take a lock so nothing changes while it runs
choices.why: That stops the system to serve a report, and readers never needed a lock here.

prompt: Somebody asks for the test environment to be made the same size as production, so that plans there are evidence. What has that request just spent?
hint: Count machines rather than servers.

choices.text: Nothing; test environments are exempt
choices.why: The exceptions Oracle publishes are narrow, and assuming one applies is how a bill arrives.

choices.text: Another licence, sized like the first one
choices.why: The metric is per core on the machine, so a second machine of the same shape costs the same again.

choices.text: A share of the support fee only
choices.why: Support is a percentage of a licence that would first have to be bought.

choices.text: Nothing, if it runs the free edition
choices.why: Then its limits make its plans evidence about a different system.

prompt: A system's business logic is a thousand stored packages. Which of the costs this lesson names is about people rather than about code?
hint: Three of the four are properties of the code itself.

choices.text: It is hard to test, needing a database and a framework
choices.why: A property of the code and its loop.

choices.text: The deployed version lives in the database
choices.why: Also about the code, and about where it sits.

choices.text: Hiring somebody who writes it well gets harder every year
choices.why: It is a risk to the system rather than a matter of taste, and no rewrite of the code removes it.

choices.text: It is one vendor's language and does not port
choices.why: A property of the language, and it is what makes a migration the project it is.

prompt: An application writes an empty string into a `city` column to mean "not given". The column is declared `NOT NULL` and the database is Oracle. What happens?
hint: Ask what that value is, there, before the constraint looks at it.

choices.text: It is stored, and reads back as an empty string
choices.why: That is every other engine in this course, and it is what the application was written against.

choices.text: It is stored, and `IS NULL` is true for it
choices.why: The constraint is what decides first, and it does not allow the row through.

choices.text: The insert is refused, because there is nothing there
choices.why: An empty string is null on that engine, so a column that may not be empty refuses it.

choices.text: It is stored as a single space, which is the old behaviour
choices.why: Nothing pads it; the value is simply absent.

prompt: Oracle exposes its internal state — the statements in the shared pool, who is connected, which locks are held — as views whose names all begin the same way. Write those two characters.
hint: One letter and one symbol.

prompt: On Oracle the two quote marks with nothing between them are not a value of length zero. Write, in one word, what they are instead.
hint: It is the thing lesson 1 spent a section on.

prompt: Match each separately-priced Oracle option to what it is on PostgreSQL.
hint: Two of them are things you have never had to ask for.

pairs.left: Splitting a large table by range or list
The performance history and session sampler
pairs.right: An extension that ships with it, and free

pairs.left: A standby you are allowed to read from

right_distractors: Not available at all, at any price
